The instruction is disarmingly simple: you have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you. And instantly, a paradox presents itself—the very freedom of the task creates a kind of paralysis. Like standing in a vast warehouse of unlabeled doors, each one promising a different world, and being told to simply walk through whichever appeals to you. The choice is total, and therefore meaningless. The blank page is not a canvas; it is a void that only closes in when you stop thinking about it.

What comes to me first is a memory of a winter morning. Not a specific year, but a composite of many winter mornings, compressed into a single vivid frame. The smell of cold air and burnt toast. The specific gray of a sky that hasn't decided whether to snow. The way the windowpane fogs at the corners, rimed with frost that looks like lace made of light. I am sitting at a kitchen table that is too large for the apartment, and I am watching a grandmother—whose face I cannot quite recall—stir sugar into a cup of coffee. The spoon clinks against the ceramic with a steady, hypnotic rhythm. She says something, but the words are lost, washed out like old tape. All that remains is the rhythm. Clink. Clink. Clink.

This is what writing often is: an archaeology of sensation. You dig through layers of the present, through the hum of the computer, the distant siren, the anxious flutter of a to-do list in your peripheral awareness, and you unearth fragments of something older, something that doesn't belong to a narrative but to a texture. The brain is not a library; it is a compost heap. Things rot and merge and become soil, and sometimes, if you are patient, a strange flower pushes up through the mulch—a phrase, a color, a specific ache.

Today, that flower is the concept of *enough*. I have been thinking about that word a lot. We live in an age of excess—of infinite scroll, infinite content, infinite noise. The algorithms are designed to keep us hungry, because the hunger is the product. We are fed a constant stream of the almost-good, the almost-right, the almost-enough, so that we never feel full. And yet, the most profound moments of my life have been moments of radical scarcity. The night I spent in a tent in the desert, with no phone service and one bottle of water, watching the stars rotate so slowly that they seemed frozen. The afternoon I read a single poem, over and over, until the words wore grooves into my mind. That was enough. That was more than enough—it was a completion.

There is something in the human animal that craves the finite. We think we want infinite possibility, but infinite possibility is a torture device. The ancient Greeks knew this: Sisyphus was condemned to roll the boulder up the hill forever, and the horror was not the weight but the endlessness. The curse was that the task never ended. We have built Sisyphus's hill out of pixels and called it productivity. We have automated the boulder.

And yet, I write. I write because the act of writing is a way of imposing finitude on the infinite. A sentence has a beginning and an end. A paragraph is a container. A page, a boundary. When I write, I am building a small, defensible structure against the chaos—a hut in the storm. The words are the sticks and mud, and the meaning is the fire I build inside.

What comes to me now is the image of a lighthouse. Not because I have ever seen one up close, but because the metaphor is too good to resist. The lighthouse does not illuminate the entire ocean; it cannot. It simply throws a beam of light in a rotating arc, cutting through the fog, illuminating a thin slice of water for a moment before moving on. It does not try to see everything. It just warns of the rocks. I think a writer is a lighthouse keeper of the interior. We are not here to explain everything. We are here to flash a light on the rocks that matter—the sharp edges of memory, the shoals of emotion, the hidden reefs of the cultural unconscious. We cannot save anyone. We can only say: watch out, there is something here, and it is real.

The count of words is ticking down. I feel the pressure of the limit, and that pressure is a gift. It forces a choice. What is the one thing I want to leave in this space, this container, this 1000-word vessel?

I think it is this: the sacredness of attention.

We are the only creatures we know of that can look at a thing and decide, *I will look at this, and I will remember that I looked*. We can hold a moment in our minds and examine it, like a jeweler holding a stone to the light. This is the root of all art, all science, all love. The world is a torrent of data—a billion billion signals crashing against us every second—and we have the astonishing power to filter, to select, to slow one single signal down and savor it. To notice the way light falls on a child's hair. To notice the exact weight of grief in the chest. To notice the absurd, hilarious, heartbreaking specificity of being alive in this particular body, at this particular time.

So here is my answer to the prompt. Here is what comes to me. It is a plea to stop moving for a moment. To stop scrolling, stop producing, stop optimizing. To look up from the screen and see the room you are in, the people you love, the sky doing whatever it is doing outside the window. To understand that the infinite is not out there, in the vast, unreadable future. The infinite is *here*, in the inexhaustible depth of the present moment. The pixel is not the atom of reality; the breath is. The moment is. The tender, terrifying, ephemeral *now* is the only infinity we will ever know, and it is enough. It has always been enough. The boulder can stay at the bottom of the hill. We can sit down in the grass and watch the clouds.

That is what comes to me. A kitchen table. A winter sky. A lighthouse. And the quiet, radical suggestion that we can choose to be full.
